No.45

Is the Bodhisattva's Wish to Save Beings a Kind of Desire? A Soul-Searching Question From Kevin Tsai

A vow has direction, desire has grasping — reflecting on the difference between a great vow and craving.

Author's record · translated; the Chinese original is authoritative

Open in reading mode →

🔶Inquiry to Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva

I asked Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva:

In an interview, Kevin Tsai (Cai Kangyong) once said publicly that he wanted to ask the Bodhisattva: isn't wanting to deliver all beings itself a desire?

If you have a desire, won't you feel frustrated at the moments it is not fulfilled?

🔶The Bodhisattva's Teaching

There are two kinds of wanting: one is grasping, one is a great vow. They share the name of desire, but the heart is different. If you want fame and gain, seeking them for yourself, you resent it when you do not get it, and fear losing it once you have it — this desire binds. If you vow that beings may leave suffering and find happiness, though you wish it accomplished, you do not force it by your own strength; though you seek and do not attain, you do not retreat from goodness. Therefore a great vow is not the same as craving.

A vow has direction; desire has grasping. A vow can let go of the result; desire must seize the result. When a Bodhisattva makes a vow, it is not that they want no result, but that they are not bound by the result. If you try to deliver beings and they are not delivered, you still do not lose compassion; if you do good and no one knows, you still wish to do good; if you seek the Dharma and have not yet realized it, you still do not turn back. This is a vow.

If your heart wishes to deliver beings only to prove yourself, only to accomplish yourself, only to receive the praise of beings, then though your mouth speaks of compassion, your heart is still grasping. So do not ask whether there is desire or not; ask this heart: Is it for myself, or for others? Clinging to results, or practicing the vow? If, when a vow is not fulfilled, you can rest at peace; if, when seeking is not fulfilled, you give rise to anger — the difference between them can be seen right here.

When beings do good, they may at first have something they seek; when Bodhisattvas make vows, they too are not without seeking. Only, as practice goes deeper, they gradually leave the self and gradually leave gaining. If a thought of compassion still holds a seeking heart, do not rush to blame yourself; simply see it clearly, and gradually let it go. True non-seeking is not wishing for nothing; it is vowing without being bound, acting without clinging.

🔶Plain Rendering

There are two kinds of desire: one is "grasping", and one is a "great vow". Although both are called "desire", the nature of the heart behind them is different. If you pursue fame and gain, seeking them for yourself, you complain when you do not get them and fear losing them when you do — this kind of desire binds you. If you vow to help beings leave suffering and find happiness, though you hope it will come true, you do not use your own force to demand the result; even if it does not happen, you do not lose your good heart because of it. So a great vow is not the same as greed.

A vow has a direction; a desire has grasping. A vow can let go of the result; a desire must hold on to the result. When Bodhisattvas make vows, it is not that they do not want results, but that they are not tied up by results. If you try to help beings across and do not succeed, you still do not lose compassion; if you do good and no one knows, you still want to keep doing good; if you seek the Dharma and have not yet realized it, you still do not turn back. This is what a vow is.

If you want to help beings only to prove yourself, only to achieve something for yourself, only to win people's praise, then even if your mouth speaks of compassion, your heart is still grasping. So do not ask "do I have desire or not?" Ask your own heart: Is it for me, or for others? Am I clinging to the result, or living out the vow? If you can stay at peace when a vow is not fulfilled, but become angry when what you sought is not obtained — the difference between the two can be seen right there.

When people do good, it is fine to want something at first; when Bodhisattvas make vows, they are not completely without wishes either. It is only that, as practice deepens, one gradually moves away from "me" and away from "getting". If a compassionate thought still carries a wish to get something, do not rush to blame yourself; just see it, and gradually let it go. True "seeking nothing" is not wanting nothing at all;

it is "vowing without being bound, acting without clinging" — having a vow but not being tied by it; taking action but not clinging to the result.
